extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism researchers, newsroom managers, and communication professionals interested in influences on news content
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating influences on TV news content
extracted.subtask_description: Rubric and measurement criteria for assessing how forces (extramedia, organizational, within-media) influence television news content and instances of agenda cutting, based primarily on reporters' perceptions from survey data. Includes operational definitions, construct composition, measurement notes, and suggested analytic approaches (correlations, regressions, controls for market size).

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall Influences on News Content and Coverage Decisions (Dependent Variable)
rubrics_metrics.description: The main dependent variable of the study representing reporters' perceptions of influences on television news content and coverage decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured via reporter survey items that ask about instances of influences on content; used as the primary outcome in correlation and regression analyses; final validated model reportedly explained 90% of the variance in this construct (based on the full data set, n=612). Treat as perception-based rather than direct content analysis; recommended to replicate with additional data types for robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staff Size Pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: A measure based on two survey questions assessing reporters' opinions of an inadequate or reduced staff size and its effects on news coverage (this indicator reflects reporters' perceptions, not actual staffing levels at their station).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positively correlated with public relations pressures and with Overall Influences on News Content; logic: inadequate staff leads to greater reliance on information subsidies and outside sources. Effect sizes were small; used reporters' generalized views of TV stations to elicit candid responses. Researchers are advised to add more measures (and possibly objective staffing data) in future work; staff size pressures explained little unique variance and was excluded from the most parsimonious organizational model but still contributed jointly with other measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Relations Pressures (PR pressures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pressures exerted by public relations practitioners/public affairs offices, often operationalized via information subsidies (e.g., press releases, video news releases) provided to stations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Found to be positively correlated with staff size pressures and to be the second-strongest extramedia predictor of Overall Influences on Content and of agenda cutting. Interpretation: smaller or understaffed newsrooms may rely on PR materials. Measurement caution: PR pressures can be conflated with communications from PIOs; suggested remedies include tracking the origin of communications or logging caller/source types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertiser Pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: Pressures exerted by advertisers on news organizations (e.g., through ad-pulling, implicit expectations), measured by reporters' perceptions of advertiser influence on coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identified as the strongest extramedia predictor of Overall Influences on Content and the strongest predictor of instances of agenda cutting. Supported by prior empirical and anecdotal evidence. Market Size relationships and sample composition may moderate this effect; researchers should note potential business-driven incentives for managers and consider advertiser influence when modeling content outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political/Government Official Pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: Pressures from politicians and government officials (and their representatives) upon news organizations, as perceived by reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally exhibited the least influence among extramedia measures within this study; sometimes made no significant contribution and was excluded from final regression models for agenda cutting. Measurement is difficult because tactics overlap with PR practitioners (PIOs), and reporters may misattribute sources; suggested approaches include content-level tracking of received communications or logging caller/source metadata to better discriminate this source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Owner / Top-level Executive Pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: Pressures coming from corporate owners or top-level executives within news organizations, as perceived by reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Found to be the strongest organizational predictor of Overall Influences on News Content and of agenda-cutting occurrences. Journalists reported significant instances where owners influence decisions about which stories to cover or emphasize. Managers and scholars should treat owner pressures as a central organizational-level force; policy implications include evidence for revising policies/procedures regarding use of externally provided materials and staffing arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic Pressures (Bottom-line pressures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial and economic pressures faced by news organizations (e.g., financial constraints, bottom-line considerations) perceived to influence content and coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Served as the second-strongest organizational predictor (after owner/executive pressures) for both Overall Influences on Content and agenda cutting. Linked in analysis to market incentives and managerial loyalties to advertisers; scholars should include economic measures when modeling organizational influence and consider interactions with ownership and staffing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extramedia Influences (Construct)
rubrics_metrics.description: An aggregate construct comprising outside-the-media forces: advertiser pressures, public relations pressures, and political/government official pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeled as directly affecting Organizational Influences and, in turn, content; examining contribution of each extramedia component (via incremental/regression analyses) is recommended to determine relative strengths (advertisers > PR > political in this study). Use both joint-construct and component-level analyses to clarify mechanisms and for agenda-cutting examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational Influences (Construct)
rubrics_metrics.description: An aggregate construct that includes internal organizational forces: staff size pressures, economic pressures, and owner/executive pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shown to directly affect Within-Media Influences and news content (i.e., without being fully mediated by newsroom managers). Owner/executive and economic pressures were the dominant contributors; staff size pressures contributed mainly in combination with others. Researchers should analyze both the combined construct and component measures to assess incremental explanatory power for content outcomes and agenda cutting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Within-Media Influences (Newsroom-level influences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources of influence located within the news organization itself, such as newsroom managers and editors (distinct from organizational-level owner/executive and economic pressures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treated as a separate level in the IOMC model that is influenced by Organizational Influences and that in turn affects news content. Although less detailed on this page, the rubric assumes measurement of managerial directives or newsroom practices separate from owner/economic/staff pressures; include measures of newsroom managerial behavior in models to capture mediation pathways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market Size (Control Variable)
rubrics_metrics.description: The size of the respondents' media market (DMA) used as a control variable to assess whether relationships between influence measures and content outcomes vary by market size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a control in correlational and regression analyses. Findings: Market Size had varying relationships (negative with advertiser pressures, positive with political pressures, no relationship with PR pressures) and had little effect on some correlations; reported effect sizes were small possibly due to sample skew toward larger DMAs. Researchers should carefully sample across market sizes and consider interactions/moderation by market size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda Cutting (Operational definition and measurement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A content-influence phenomenon defined as (1) placing an item low on the news agenda (buried), (2) removing an item from the agenda once present, or (3) ignoring/not covering a story or topic in the first place; measured in this study primarily via reporters' reports of ignoring/not covering stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treated as a specific outcome related to content influence, distinct from agenda setting. Analyses showed agenda cutting is real and more strongly predicted by extramedia and organizational measures—especially advertiser and owner/executive pressures—than general content influence. Researchers are encouraged to develop more facets of agenda cutting (beyond 'ignoring') and to use experimental, longitudinal, or pre-designed surveys to assess audience effects and causal mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement Approach: Reporter Perceptions vs Objective/Tactical Data
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological rubric point emphasizing that measures in this study are perception-based (reporters' opinions about pressures at TV stations in general), not necessarily objective measures of practices or actual communications received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perception-based measurement can elicit candid responses about influences but may conflate sources (e.g., PR vs PIO) and is subject to bias. Suggested methodological remedies: collect objective data on communications tactics (e.g., VNRs, releases), log caller/source types, or supplement surveys with content analyses or station-level records to triangulate findings and better identify origins of pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incremental Strength Assessment and Analytic Strategy (Regression/Correlation Guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytic rubric for determining relative contribution of influence measures: use correlations and multiple regression to evaluate incremental strength of extramedia and organizational predictors for Overall Influences on Content and for agenda cutting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare joint-construct models (e.g., overall Extramedia) and component-level models (advertiser, PR, political) to identify strongest predictors; test models controlling for Market Size and other covariates; exclude non-significant predictors for parsimonious models but report their joint contributions. Note small effect sizes may reflect sample composition; replication with more representative sampling recommended.
